name: Tomas Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tomas, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach PE, mostly, at Brookfield High, a town secondary school, and I pick up a few geography lessons with Year 8 to fill my timetable. So my day is changing rooms, whistles, bibs that smell of wet dog, and then a classroom with maps after lunch. I coach the under-15 football team on Wednesdays and we got to the county semi-final last year. What wears me out is rainy days, when thirty kids are crammed in the sports hall doing badminton.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside school? Home life, money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented one-bed flat over a dentist's, ten minutes' walk from school. I've got about four months of bills put by, and I play Sunday league with some lads from uni. I don't use the AI stuff at all. I'm not against it exactly; I just haven't needed it, and I've seen what it does to kids' homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never got the fuss. I'd probably say it in the PE office and then nobody would mention it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes for me, which is fine. PE doesn't run on screens, and my geography lessons are a small slice. My pay's ordinary but it covers the flat and football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on. I'd keep putting a hundred a month in savings, maybe go for my next coaching badge. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit relieved I didn't waste time learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that bothers you about work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sports hall roof leaks, and they keep saying there's no money to fix it. That's my biggest work worry, and it's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've seen what AI does to homework. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year 8s handing in geography homework that sounds like a textbook from a robot. A twelve-year-old doesn't write 'furthermore' about volcanoes. It's lazy, and it wastes my time checking.

say: I'd say I **never got the fuss** about AI in the first place.
I'd mention it once in the **PE office** and then let it drop.
think: I think **nothing changes** for me, since PE doesn't run on screens.
My pay is **ordinary** but covers the flat and Sunday football.
do: Keep teaching **PE and geography** exactly as now.
feel: **Calm**, and a little relieved he didn't waste time learning the tools.
S0.quote: A twelve-year-old doesn't write 'furthermore' about volcanoes.
fieldNote: His job is mostly **hands-on PE**, which the plateau doesn't touch.
Biggest work worry is a **leaking sports hall** roof, unrelated to AI.
Mild **irritation** at AI-written homework shapes his view of the tools.

steps.text: Keep teaching PE and Year 8 geography as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see how it goes. Some things will get easier, some will get worse, and I'm not going to pretend I know which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the geography side changes: lesson plans and marking done by software, maybe even the explaining. But PE's fine. You can't learn to take a penalty from a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much in year one. I'd wait and see what the school actually wants. If they push AI for geography, I'd ask the head for a full PE timetable instead, which I'd prefer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like when the fixtures list changes and you're not sure who you're playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your geography lessons are the thinking part. What happens to those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably they'd want them on some platform where the AI does the explaining and I walk round. I'd hate that. I'm good at the bit where you draw a river on the board and kids get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have to use the tools then, wouldn't you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they make me, yes, but only the bare minimum. I'd get a colleague to show me. I'm not going to go home and practise.

say: I'd say **let's see** how it goes rather than pretend I know.
Some things will get **easier** and some will get **worse**.
think: I think the **geography side** changes, with software doing planning and marking.
PE stays fine, because you can't learn a **penalty** from a chatbot.
do: **Wait** to see what the school actually asks for in year one.
Ask the head for a **full PE timetable** if geography moves onto AI.
Use AI only when **forced**, with a colleague showing me.
feel: **Slightly uneasy**, like a fixtures list changing without warning.
S1.quote: You can't learn to take a penalty from a chatbot.
fieldNote: He shields himself by **moving fully into PE**, the hands-on side.
Resists tools but would comply with the **bare minimum**.
Pride in **whiteboard teaching** shows what he'd miss in geography.

steps.text: Wait for the school's AI plan before changing anything
Ask the head for a full PE timetable instead of geography

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people are panicking and I'd want someone sensible in charge, from whatever party. I'd keep my head down at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my geography lessons would go first, and that's a chunk of my timetable. PE probably lasts a few years, but schools under pressure might merge PE groups or hand them to coaches on lower pay. I'd be worried about hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on the extras, like the new boots and the lads' weekend away. I'd build savings up as fast as I could, maybe up to six months. And I'd ask to go full-time PE so geography doesn't drag me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can feel my shoulders go up just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2031. What does that mean for PE?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031, maybe. But a robot that can stop a kid getting a football in the face and tie a fourteen-year-old's ankle strapping? I'd believe it when I see it. Parents want a person on the touchline, whatever the robots can do by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're on your own. Who would you lean on if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum and dad, two hours away. Their spare room's there. I wouldn't like it at twenty-nine, but I'd go.

say: I'd say people are **panicking** and we need sensible leaders from any party.
I'd keep my **head down** at work.
think: I think my **geography lessons** go first, a real chunk of my timetable.
Schools under pressure might give PE to **cheaper coaches**, cutting my hours.
do: Cut **extras** like new boots and the lads' weekend away.
Build savings up to **six months** as fast as possible.
Ask to go **full-time PE** before geography is cut.
feel: **Anxious**, with tension he can feel in his shoulders.
S2.quote: Parents want a person on the touchline, whatever the robots can do by 2031.
fieldNote: He sees **lost hours**, not total job loss, because PE is hands-on.
Doubts robots can manage **kids' safety** on a field, even after 2031.
Fallback is **parents' spare room**, which he'd accept reluctantly.

steps.text: Skip new football boots and the lads' weekend away
Build savings to six months of bills
Ask the head to make his timetable full-time PE
Move into his parents' spare room if hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to work it out, so let's not get hysterical. I'd say that to the lads at football too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm fine for a good while. PE stays human longest, and robots wouldn't come till 2034. I'd be thirty-five, still young enough to change if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my next coaching badge in the next year or two, because coaching clubs is a job that stays with people. I'd keep saving. Otherwise I'd wait for things to get clearer before I did anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years to see it coming, would you do anything differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know what to retrain into. Everyone said learn to code, and now coding is the first thing to go. I'd rather wait and see what actually lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would retrain now. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going full-time PE, yes, if geography gets taken. I'd ask early, before the timetable for 2031 gets written.

say: I'd say there's **time** to work it out, so nobody should get hysterical.
I'd say the same to the lads at **Sunday football**.
think: I think **PE stays human** longest, with robots not arriving till 2034.
At **thirty-five** I'd still be young enough to change if needed.
do: Take my next **coaching badge** within two years.
Ask early to go **full-time PE** before the 2031 timetable is set.
feel: **Uneasy**, but not losing sleep over it.
S3.quote: Everyone said learn to code, and now coding is the first thing to go.
fieldNote: His reluctance to retrain comes from **distrust of advice** like 'learn to code'.
Treats a **coaching badge** as low-risk insurance.
Expects the **robot delay** to protect his hands-on work into his mid-thirties.

steps.text: Take the next football coaching badge within two years
Hold off big career changes until the picture is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time. Plenty can change, and it might not even happen like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think that's so far off I can't plan for it. By 2039, when robots arrive, I'd be forty and probably head of PE somewhere, with kids myself maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Coaching badge, steady saving, the usual. I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Ten years is ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out, you'd be thirty-seven. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, actually. Head of PE, running the football, maybe a wife and a small kid by then. I don't see a robot taking a minibus of teenagers to an away game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this that would change your mind about learning AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if the school made it part of my job and I saw it working for colleagues. I'm not stubborn for the sake of it. I just don't jump first.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and plenty can change.
It might not even **happen** that way.
think: I think it's too **far off** to plan for.
By 2039 I'd probably be **head of PE**, maybe with a family.
do: Carry on teaching and coaching **as usual**.
Finish the **coaching badge** and keep steady saving.
**Wait and see** before any bigger change.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years feels like a long way off.
S4.quote: I don't see a robot taking a minibus of teenagers to an away game.
fieldNote: The decade **removes urgency** for him almost completely.
He'd adopt tools only once **colleagues prove** them, never first.
His future picture is **head of PE**, family, football.

steps.text: Keep teaching PE and coaching the under-15s
Wait for proof before learning any AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the geography hours fast and wouldn't have a plan. What would help is the school letting PE staff go full-time PE, and some help with retraining that's actually about something that lasts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the kids. They're the ones who'll grow up in this. I'd rather kids knew how to lose a football match well than how to ask a computer for an essay.

headlineQuote: I'd rather kids knew how to lose a football match well than how to ask a computer for an essay.
portrait: Tomas teaches **PE** at a town secondary and fills his timetable with Year 8 geography.
He lives **alone** in a rented flat, saves steadily and plays Sunday league football.
He's never used AI and **waits** for proof before changing anything.
He's calm in the plateau, **anxious** at AGI by 2028 over lost geography hours.
His plan is to go **full-time PE** and take coaching badges, betting hands-on work lasts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose geography hours fast with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining help aimed at **work that lasts**.
